title: The Novel Imagining Life After a Second Civil War
gist: Emily St. John Mandel's new novel Exit Party imagines a fractured, seceded United States after a 2031 coup and civil war, reflecting what the reviewers call a broader cultural trend of 'serious thinkers from across the political spectrum' now openly discussing the possibility of a second U.S. civil war or societal collapse.

themes.theme: Civil-war and collapse fiction as a cultural bellwether

insights.claim: The reviewers note it is 'striking' that, in recent years, serious thinkers across the political spectrum have begun warning of the possibility of a second U.S. civil war or societal collapse, a shift they treat as a meaningful departure from America's traditional self-image as a country of 'relentless optimism.'
insights.speaker: Chloe Hadavas, Allison Meakem
insights.so_what: Mainstream literary and political discourse increasingly treating U.S. societal collapse as a plausible scenario (not fringe speculation) is itself a soft sentiment indicator worth tracking alongside polling and political-risk models on U.S. institutional stability.
insights.quote: it's striking that, in recent years, serious thinkers from across the political spectrum have taken to warning of the possibility of a second civil war, or some other form of U.S. societal collapse.
insights.locator: The United States is known as a country of relentless

insights.claim: Emily St. John Mandel's Exit Party opens in Los Angeles in 2031 after a coup d'état splinters the United States, with California having seceded into its own stable but unaffordable 'Republic,' while much of the rest of the country degenerates into militia-controlled city-states operating out of former Staples stores and shopping malls.
insights.speaker: Chloe Hadavas, Allison Meakem
insights.so_what: The specific fictional detail that a stable post-collapse California becomes 'unaffordable' echoes real current U.S. regional cost-of-living divergence, an intentional authorial commentary worth noting for how creative works are processing present-day economic anxieties.
insights.quote: The Republic of California is now its own country... and therefore unaffordable
insights.locator: Mandel—who, I should note, is Canadian—begins Exit Party

insights.claim: Mandel's prior dystopian novel, Station Eleven (2014), depicted a pandemic-devastated world and gained a surge of new readership and an HBO adaptation six years later — after the real 2020 COVID-19 pandemic — establishing her reputation as, in the reviewers' words, 'an unwitting forecaster of very real geopolitical crises.'
insights.speaker: Chloe Hadavas, Allison Meakem
insights.so_what: Illustrates how speculative fiction can gain retrospective cultural authority when real events validate its scenarios — a dynamic that may amplify public reception and media attention around Exit Party's civil-war premise regardless of its predictive accuracy.

insights.claim: In the novel's alternate totalitarian-future branch, the 'United State' achieves prosperity and public health gains (cancer immunization, bullet trains) through pervasive surveillance and a Stasi-like secret police, presenting the trade-off between order/security and freedom as symmetric with the chaotic-secession branch rather than clearly preferable.
insights.speaker: Chloe Hadavas, Allison Meakem
insights.so_what: The novel's even-handed treatment of authoritarian order versus fragmented chaos as both flawed outcomes reflects a cultural mental model in which neither centralized control nor decentralization is seen as a safe resolution to institutional breakdown.
insights.quote: There was a world where my homeland had fractured into disarray, and another where my homeland had closed like a fist.

themes.theme: Companion themes: climate domes and elite escapism

insights.claim: Ben Eastham's debut novel The Floating World depicts a billionaire arms-manufacturing heir resurrecting an abandoned Greek island mining settlement as a climate-haven community under a giant dome, described in the text as a 'doomsday bunker for billionaires' and 'insurance against the end of the world.'
insights.speaker: Chloe Hadavas, Allison Meakem
insights.so_what: Reinforces a recurring cultural theme (also present in Exit Party) of billionaire-funded climate-refuge enclaves as an emerging speculative-fiction trope, mirroring real-world reporting on ultra-wealthy climate bunker investment.
insights.quote: a sustainable, holistic, homeostatic community for powerful people who want insurance against the end of the world.
insights.locator: This recently widowed narrator has left London
